candidate.state: uncommitted working tree on base; measured source hashes below. RequestLatencyMeasurementSpec.hs later gained the RequestPlanModes example and a spreadHistory helper extracted unchanged from the measured path; its hash is the final file.

retention: Retain this compact receipt until a matched rerun, a production sample or a qualified timeline, pool, discovery or change-stream change supersedes it. Generated logs, plan logs, sandbox databases and raw summaries were task scratch and were removed after the run. The container environment, its logs and summaries are scratch under .tmp/perftest and Docker resources named hmem-perftest*, retained for the later tasks of this project and removed by the last of them.
method: Opt-in hspec measurement in hmem-server RequestLatencyMeasurementSpec. The real application (local auth, production middleware order including the metadata-only request logger and its phase fields) runs on Warp over loopback with a production-default pool (10 connections, 60 s idle, 30 s statement timeout, 127.0.0.1 DSN) against an isolated native PostgreSQL test cluster. A fixed-seed (0x9bb3fedd, SplitMix64) workspace of the large perf fixture shape is created through HTTP; audit history is spread over 90 days and VACUUM ANALYZE refreshes statistics. Twenty route variants run in a pool-cold sequential pass (200 rounds; the first sample per variant is reported as cold) and in concurrent profiles of 4 and 16 clients with disjoint write targets; the 16-client profile is repeated against a one-stripe pool and then against the production pool again. Each phase records request-log phases joined by X-Request-Id, process checkout counters, pg_stat_activity and pg_locks samples every 25 ms, pg_stat_database deltas and pg_stat_statements. Matched plans come from auto_explain (analyze) on fresh connections for the six slowest sequential variants; a separate RequestPlanModes probe runs nine variants eight times on one connection under plan_cache_mode auto and force_custom_plan. Times are monotonic; app is complete minus wait, hold and provider time.

matchedPlans.evidence: Nested loop left joins between MATERIALIZED CTE scans estimated at one row remove 1,043,478 to 1,937,031 rows by join filter (2,000 eligible Observations against 522 to 969 FTS-ranked rows), about 95% of 557 to 642 ms. No temp files; shared buffer hits only.
The same join pattern removes 2,738,220 to 2,876,636 rows (1,411 to 1,448 eligible rows, 415 to 423 ms) when half of the Observations match; 10 ms when none match.

Custom plans (executions 2 to 5 on a connection) use hash joins in 21 ms. From the sixth execution the generic plan estimates one row for the ($4 IS NULL OR ...) range predicates and uses nested loops with a sequential projects scan per row (475,625 and 275,882 rows removed by join filter), 218 to 225 ms.

matchedPlans.statement: Timeline buckets (WITH bounds), day buckets over 92 days
matchedPlans.evidence: 309 ms: a per-bucket nested loop over 6,218 inventory deltas (93 loops, 240,427 rows removed) and inventory CTE materialization that spills about 2,014 temp blocks (16 MB) per call.

observations: Sequential tails are database execution: mean hold is at least 96% of mean request time for every variant above 20 ms, mean pool wait is at most 0.05 ms except while connections are created, and the application residual is at most 3.4 ms.
Observation discovery is the slowest interactive route (538 ms p50, 653 to 807 ms p99, n=199); its subject-tree view is bimodal (6 ms p50, 346 ms p95).

Timeline events take 234 ms p50 sequentially but 21 to 44 ms with custom plans; the prepared generic plan is the whole difference. Forcing custom plans everywhere slowed day buckets (about 255 to 340 ms) and task updates, so the effect is statement-specific.
Timeline buckets take 140 ms (week, all time) and 247 ms (day). The sequential phase wrote 1,194 temp files (8.2 GB), consistent with about 14 MB spilled per bucket call.

With only 4 clients (at most 3 active backends) 2,652 of 11,716 checkouts were capacity waits behind a full one-connection stripe, and checkout wait totalled 111 s in a 112 s phase. Batch, root and project navigation p95 rose from 15 to 51 ms to 0.94 to 1.97 s with at least 97% of tail time spent waiting for a connection (navigation focus 14 to 95 ms, 96%).

The same 16-client profile finished in 33.7 s with one stripe against 55.2 s and 48.2 s with production striping, and capacity waits fell from 206 and 548 to 1, but latency was mixed. Against the first 16-client run, p95 ranged from 4.3 times higher (planning_counts 24 to 104 ms) to 7.3 times lower (nav_root 1,445 to 198 ms): task_list_query (64 to 105 ms) and task_update_status (381 to 408 ms) also got worse, nav_focus improved only 1.3 times (674 to 507 ms), and against the repeat run timeline_buckets_day and timeline_events were also slower. p50 rose for every database route except search_unified and nav_root (task_get 9 to 32 ms). One stripe is not a clear win.

Requests make many checkouts: 9 to 10 per task update, 28 per navigation batch, 5 per navigation root and 6 per unified search including three concurrent branches. Waits multiply with checkouts under contention.
Each task update (36 ms p50) executes hmem_projects_have_paused_ancestry about 69 times (27,609 calls for 400 updates).
Lock activity is minor: lock waits, all advisory, in at most 94 of 1,099 activity samples (126 advisory wait events), at most 3 ungranted locks, no deadlocks and no heap reads (blks_read 0).
The run opened 34 connections. A direct connect averaged 47.9 ms on 127.0.0.1 and 66.5 ms (max 226 ms) on localhost; the first sequential request of a variant paid up to 219 ms of connection time.

containerSample.method: Six workspaces of the large perf shape (the SplitMix64 generator of RequestLatencyMeasurementSpec, seeds 0x9bb3fedd+i) were created through HTTP. 562 terminated and 12 active sessions of transcript-like JSONL (gzip ratio 2.45) were uploaded through the session API in 16 to 256 KiB record-aligned appends, with log-normal sizes normalised to the production totals; the server worker archived the terminated sessions. About 7,100 API task updates were made; task-update audit rows were then replicated 25 times in SQL with fresh ids, spread over 90 days, followed by VACUUM FULL audit_log and VACUUM ANALYZE. Load used the isolated route mix after one warm-up round, with disjoint write targets per client. Profiles: sequential, 4 clients, 16 clients, and 16 clients with four appenders, each sending 4 to 32 KiB to its own active session every 250 ms. Phases come from the server request log joined by X-Request-Id and from GET /api/v1/health pool.checkout deltas; pg_stat_activity and pg_locks are sampled every 25 ms inside the database container, with pg_stat_database deltas and pg_stat_statements per profile. Matched plans come from auto_explain (analyze, buffers) on a restarted server and from EXPLAIN of the outbox replay statement.

matchedPlans.statement: Timeline buckets (WITH bounds), day buckets over 92 days, 87,068 workspace audit rows
matchedPlans.evidence: 4,656 ms: a sequential scan of all 413,368 audit_log rows keeps 85,676 and removes 327,692 by filter (326,300 from other workspaces, 1,392 of the workspace's other entity types);the inventory_state_values sort spills 123,544 kB to disk; the per-bucket nested loop emits 4,000,752 rows and removes 3,966,932 by join filter over 93 buckets; 106,216 shared blocks read and 70,758 temp blocks written per call. All-time week buckets: 3,015 ms with the same shape.

workspace_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM $2 is not an index condition. The custom plan scans idx_change_stream_outbox_replay on scope and cursor only and filters 6,797 rows (7,225 buffers, 5.0 ms); the generic plan scans the whole outbox (78,854 rows, 12,645 buffers, 13.0 ms). Called about 6.2 times/s as background work during the sequential profile.

observations: Timeline buckets are the dominant tail and pool holder at this history size: 3,371 to 4,383 ms sequential p50 (n=79) against 139 to 247 ms with 5,789 audit rows. The statement was 885 s of 1,246 s pooled hold time sequentially (71%) and 84 to 85% under concurrency, writing about 430 MB of temporary files per call.

Pool wait follows the bucket holds. With 4 clients, timeline events, project navigation, the discovery subject tree, task field updates and unified search reached 1.9 to 2.9 s p95, while task status updates stayed at 101 ms; with 16 clients and capture, pool wait was 98 to 100% of the tail for every database variant except timeline buckets (48 to 56%), discovery content (83%), discovery continuation (91%) and unified search (123%, three concurrent branches). Capacity waits occurred in every profile: 1,603 sequential, 1,960 with 4 clients, 124 and 180 with 16 clients (lower bounds).

Background work is most pool traffic: unattributed checkouts were 97,933 of 107,503 sequentially (about 96/s) and 23 to 51% under load. Sequentially, background checkouts waited about 575 s in total against 3 s for requests, with 153 waits over 1 s.
Session capture appends make 6 checkouts each; under 16 clients they had 12.6 ms p50 but 3,076 ms p95, 4,239 ms p99 and 8,781 ms max (n=1,023), with 100% pool wait in the tail.
Discovery is unchanged from the isolated baseline at 523 to 527 ms p50 with over 99% hold; its subject tree remains bimodal (8 ms p50, 328 ms p95).
Timeline events took 8.9 ms p50 and 46.9 ms p99 sequentially (hold 8 ms), so the isolated generic-plan tail (234 ms p50 on PostgreSQL 18.2) did not reproduce on PostgreSQL 17.11 at this scale.
Locks: lock waits in at most 54 of 6,533 samples (advisory and transaction-id), at most 2 ungranted locks, no deadlocks. Application residual at most 7.2 ms. Connection setup 5.5 ms.

A discarded first capture profile returned 17 429 discovery_capacity responses because the runner started new discovery search sessions per profile, leaving 32 live contexts from the previous profile under the server limit of 64. The runner now reuses one search session per client and view; the rerun had no errors.
limitations: Not production: one Docker Desktop VM with PostgreSQL 17.11 and default memory settings, 5.5 ms connections instead of the native host's 47.9 ms, and synthetic data. Production request mix, concurrency, PostgreSQL version and settings remain unknown.

Scale differs per family (fixture.*.scale): archive sidecars 0.45 and outbox 0.14; production appends are probably smaller (its ledger is 8.5 times larger). Audit history is 26 copies of API task-update rows spread uniformly over 90 days; the measured workspace may hold more or less history than the busiest production workspace.
Shared buffers (128 MB) are smaller than the audit table, so bucket calls read from the VM page cache (61 million blocks read sequentially); first-touch disk reads were not measured.
Sample sizes: n=79 sequential and 80 with 4 clients (p99 is the maximum) and n=112 with 16 clients (p99 is the second-largest); tail compositions are 4 to 6 samples, 52 for appends.
No one-stripe probe in the container: the pool stripe count is not configurable without a code change.
Active sessions grew during the capture profiles after the manifest (about 2,000 appends).

limitations: No passive native sample was collected. By the user decision of 2026-11-16 the isolated Docker container sample (containerSample) replaces it; it is synthetic and not production, and its own limits are listed there. Production stripes, request mix, concurrency and planning sizes remain unmeasured.

One host, loopback HTTP and one 2,000-Observation workspace with warm shared buffers (no heap reads). The host has 24 capabilities, so the pool had 10 one-connection stripes; the production capability count decides its stripes.
Sample sizes: n=199 per sequential variant (p99 is the second-largest sample) and 100 (c4) or 128 (c16) per concurrent variant; tail compositions average 6 to 10 samples.

Run-to-run variance is material on this shared host: an earlier matched run had 2 to 6 times higher sequential p99 for discovery and timeline routes. Only this run is recorded; two earlier runs had a navigation fixture defect or no pg_stat_statements and were discarded.
The embedding provider was disabled, so discovery ran FTS-only and provider_ms was never set. Hybrid discovery and provider latency are unmeasured.
pg_stat_statements with track=all and track_io_timing add overhead; auto_explain analyze inflates plan-probe times; 25 ms pg_stat_activity samples undercount short lock waits.
capacity_waits is a process-wide lower bound. Work forked without the request timer is unattributed (none in this run).

The health check's non-blocking probe is not a checkout, but a connection it opens counts in connects, connect_total_ms and that request's db_connect_ms with zero db_checkouts and db_wait_ms (health coldMs: 220.2 ms complete, 218.9 ms connect).
